prompt: On pc1, ethtool -i eth0 printed driver: veth. What does that tell you about the card?
hint: The lab is one Linux computer.

choices.text: It is a Wi-Fi radio
choices.why: A radio would show a wireless driver; this one is a pair of virtual cards.

choices.text: Its driver failed to load
choices.why: A card whose driver failed would not be UP and passing pings.

choices.text: It is a virtual Ethernet pair
choices.why: Right. veth is the lab's card and cable in software.

choices.text: It is a USB adapter on the main board
choices.why: There is no hardware here at all; bus-info is empty.

prompt: pc1's RX packets counter read 22 before five pings to the server and 29 after. How many frames did the card receive in between?
hint: Subtract.

prompt: pc1 sent five pings, and its TX packets counter rose by 6. Every ping was answered. What is the sixth frame?
hint: The neighbour table had been emptied.

choices.text: An ARP request
choices.why: Right. pc1 had to ask for the server's MAC before the first ping left.

choices.text: A ping sent again after a loss
choices.why: The summary says 5 received and 0% packet loss.

choices.text: A collision counted as a frame
choices.why: collsns stayed at 0, and collisions are not counted as packets.

choices.text: The ping summary printed to the screen
choices.why: The summary is text in the terminal, not a frame on the cable.

prompt: A user says their link has been slow all morning. ip -s link shows errors 1532 on RX. One minute later it still says 1532, and again a minute after that. What does that tell you?
hint: A counter is a total since the card came up.

choices.text: The cable is damaged right now
choices.why: Then the number would be climbing between the readings.

choices.text: The errors are history; the slowness is elsewhere
choices.why: Right. A number that does not move is not the current fault.

choices.text: The router is dropping the user's packets
choices.why: A router's drops are not counted by the user's card.

choices.text: 1532 errors in a morning is a normal rate
choices.why: There is no rate: the number stood still for two minutes.

prompt: How many bits long is a MAC address such as 02:25:70:bc:29:c6?
hint: Six bytes of eight bits.

prompt: Every MAC address in the lab starts with the byte 02, which is 00000010 in binary. What do its two lowest bits say?
hint: Bit 0 is I/G, bit 1 is U/L.

choices.text: A group address from manufacturer number 02
choices.why: The I/G bit is 0, so it is one card, and a local address names no maker.

choices.text: A broadcast to the whole link
choices.why: Broadcast is ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, with every bit set.

choices.text: One card, address set locally
choices.why: Right. I/G is 0 and U/L is 1.

choices.text: One card, address burnt in at the factory
choices.why: A factory address has U/L 0; here bit 1 is set.

prompt: Which of these are locally administered addresses of one card? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the second hex digit of each.

choices.why: Right. 2: U/L set, I/G clear.
Right. 0x52 ends in 2 as well, so the same two bits.

choices.text: 00:1b:21:aa:bb:cc
choices.why: 0 leaves U/L clear: a factory address.
3 sets I/G as well: a group address.
Right. e is 1110: U/L set, I/G clear.

prompt: In a MAC address burnt in at the factory, the first three bytes are the block the IEEE sold the manufacturer, called its ___.
hint: Three capital letters.

prompt: Why does the lab's script build each MAC address from 02 and a hash of the device's and interface's names?
hint: Think of a transcript recorded twice.

choices.text: Addresses starting with 02 are delivered faster
choices.why: No bit of a MAC address changes its speed.

choices.text: So each card has the same MAC on every build
choices.why: Right. Transcripts recorded on different days then match.

choices.text: Namespaces refuse a factory address
choices.why: A namespace takes any address; the choice is the lab's.

choices.text: To make every card part of one group
choices.why: 02 leaves the I/G bit clear: each is one card.

prompt: What does a repeater read from the frames it passes on?
hint: It sits at layer 1.

choices.text: The destination MAC address
choices.why: That is a bridge or a switch, at layer 2.

choices.text: The destination IP address
choices.why: That is a router, at layer 3.

choices.text: No address: it regenerates the signal
choices.why: Right. Clean signal, fresh timing, nothing decided.

choices.text: The frame's checksum, to fix errors
choices.why: It does not look inside frames at all.

prompt: What is the longest run of twisted-pair copper allowed between two Ethernet devices?
hint: It decides where the switches in a building go.

prompt: Two groups of PCs are joined by a repeater on a copper cable. A PC on one side and a PC on the other start sending at the same instant. What happens?
hint: What does a repeater do with a signal?

choices.text: The repeater keeps one frame and sends it later
choices.why: Keeping a frame means reading it, and a repeater does not.

choices.text: They collide
choices.why: Right. A repeater extends one collision domain; it does not split it.

choices.text: Nothing: each side is its own segment
choices.why: That is what a bridge gives; a repeater copies the signal across.

choices.text: The repeater drops the frame for the far side
choices.why: It cannot tell which side a frame is for.

prompt: sw1's table was empty. pc1 pinged the server once, then pc2 did. The table then held three entries. Where did the third come from?
hint: Who else sent frames in those two pings?

choices.text: From the router on p8, which forwards every ping
choices.why: These pings stayed in the office; r1 sent nothing.

choices.text: From pc3, which hears the pings
choices.why: pc3 sent nothing, so it has no entry.

choices.text: From a static entry the lab configured
choices.why: The command asked for dynamic entries, learnt ones.

choices.text: From the server's replies, on p4
choices.why: Right. It answered both, and its source MAC was learnt.

prompt: sw1 reports ageing_time 30000, in hundredths of a second. How many seconds is that?
hint: Divide by 100.

prompt: A bridge joins two halves of an Ethernet. Which does it split into two?
hint: A broadcast is for everybody.

choices.text: The collision domain, and not the broadcast domain
choices.why: Right. It receives whole frames, and still sends broadcasts out of every port.

choices.text: The broadcast domain only
choices.why: ARP's question still crosses a bridge.

choices.text: Both
choices.why: Splitting the broadcast domain takes a router, or VLANs in lesson 19.

choices.text: Neither: it is a longer cable
choices.why: That describes a repeater.

prompt: Put in order what a bridge does with a frame that arrives on one of its ports.
hint: It learns before it looks up.
items: Record its source MAC against the incoming port
Look up its destination MAC in the table
Send it out of that port, or out of every port if unknown
trap: Learning comes first: the source is recorded even when the destination is unknown, which is how the reply finds its way back.

prompt: On Linux, the command that lists what a bridge has learnt is bridge ___ show.
hint: Three letters: forwarding database.

prompt: pc1 pinged 192.0.2.80, and its capture shows the frame going to 02:1f:23:e7:e9:d5. Whose MAC address is that?
hint: The last command of the block answers it.

choices.why: That card is two networks away; its MAC never reaches pc1.

choices.text: r1's eth0, the gateway
choices.why: Right. ip -br link show eth0 on r1 printed it.

choices.text: The switch sw1
choices.why: A switch forwards frames without being their destination.

choices.text: The provider's router, isp
choices.why: isp is on the next link, beyond r1.

prompt: Why did pc1 send no ARP request for 192.0.2.80 before pinging it?
hint: Where does ARP's question reach?

choices.text: It already had 192.0.2.80 in its neighbour table
choices.why: Its table held only the server before the ping.

choices.text: ICMP needs no MAC address
choices.why: Every packet on Ethernet travels in a frame with a MAC.

choices.text: The router answered on 192.0.2.80's behalf
choices.why: No request for 192.0.2.80 was sent for anybody to answer.

choices.text: It is off-link, so pc1 asked for the gateway's MAC
choices.why: Right. ARP reaches the same link; the packet goes via 10.20.10.1.

prompt: Match each address in pc1's frame to 192.0.2.80 with what it names.
hint: Two pairs, two reaches.

pairs.right: The far end of the journey

prompt: A host is configured as 10.20.10.21/24. Which of these can be its default gateway?
hint: The host reaches its gateway by ARP.

choices.why: That is the provider, on a network the host is not on.
The third number differs: outside 10.20.10.0/24.
Right. Inside the host's own network.
Two networks away; no ARP would reach it.

prompt: In a factory, a box reads sensors on a network that does not speak IP and sends their values as IP to a server. In which sense is it a gateway?
hint: The word has two meanings.

choices.text: It is the default route of the sensors
choices.why: The sensors have no IP, so they have no routing table.

choices.text: It translates between two systems
choices.why: Right. It changes the language of the traffic, not only the network.

choices.text: It repeats the sensors' signal further
choices.why: That is a repeater; nothing is translated.

choices.text: It learns the sensors' MAC addresses
choices.why: That is a bridge, between two Ethernet segments; nothing is translated.

prompt: pc2's ping to 192.0.2.80 printed 'From 10.20.10.22 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable'. Who produced that message?
hint: Whose address is 10.20.10.22?

choices.text: The router r1
choices.why: r1 never received the packet; its address would be 10.20.10.1.

choices.text: The server 192.0.2.80
choices.why: Nothing reached it, and its address is not the one shown.

choices.text: pc2's own kernel
choices.why: Right. Its ARP for 10.20.10.254 went unanswered and it gave up.

choices.text: The switch, which found no port
choices.why: A switch floods unknown destinations; it sends no ICMP.

prompt: After the unanswered pings, ip neigh on pc2 showed the line 10.20.10.254 dev eth0 ___.
hint: The state of an address ARP asked about and nobody answered.

prompt: Match each symptom to where the fault is.
hint: Look at who sent the error.

pairs.left: Local hosts answer; 'unreachable' comes from your own address
pairs.right: The gateway address is wrong or down

pairs.left: Local hosts answer; 'unreachable' comes from the gateway
pairs.right: The gateway has no route onwards
The link or the host's own address

prompt: A whole office cannot reach the internet the morning after somebody edited the DHCP scope, though printers and file shares work. What is the first thing to check?
hint: Which setting does DHCP hand out with the address?

choices.text: The switch's MAC table
choices.why: Local traffic works, so the switch is learning and forwarding.

choices.text: The gateway in the scope
choices.why: Right. Leases renewed overnight carried it to every machine.

choices.text: The cables to each desk
choices.why: A cable fault would break the local traffic too.

choices.text: The MAC addresses of the PCs
choices.why: They did not change, and local hosts answer them.

prompt: Put in order what pc1 does to send a ping to 192.0.2.80.
hint: Route first, then the link.
items: Ask with ARP for the MAC of 10.20.10.1
Send a frame to r1's MAC holding the packet for 192.0.2.80
trap: ARP comes after the route: the host has to know which neighbour to ask about before it can ask.

prompt: An office lets only listed MAC addresses onto its Wi-Fi. A phone that worked last month is refused after joining under a new network name. What explains it?
hint: What does a phone do with its MAC on each network it joins?

choices.text: Its maker's OUI was removed from the list
choices.why: The list holds addresses; the phone's is not its factory one.

choices.text: Its MAC expired after 300 seconds
choices.why: Ageing removes table entries, not a card's address.

choices.text: It chose a new random local MAC for that network
choices.why: Right. A new address per network, so the listed one no longer matches.

choices.text: Its I/G bit is set
choices.why: A phone's address names one card.

prompt: Which of these devices read no address at all? Choose all that apply.
hint: Layer 1 only.

choices.text: A repeater
choices.why: Right. It regenerates the signal.

choices.text: A bridge
choices.why: It reads source and destination MAC.

choices.text: A hub
choices.why: Right. A repeater with several ports.

choices.text: A network card
choices.why: It keeps the frames addressed to its own MAC.

choices.text: A router
choices.why: It reads the destination IP.
